children: Guinea's President Mamady Doumbouya will play a major role in steering a sovereign wealth fund created to use revenue from the Simandou iron ore mine to generate jobs and broad economic growth, an official involved in setting up the fund told Reuters on Thursday.
Lawmakers in the West African nation unanimously approved on Wednesday a law to establish the fund and a target for it to hold $1 billion within five years, the official said.
A consortium led by China's Baowu
, the world's largest steelmaker, and a joint venture led by Rio Tinto
, is developing Simandou. It came online last year, ending decades of stalemate during which it was the world's richest untapped iron ore deposit.
The World Bank expects Simandou will lift Guinea's growth to an average of 9% in 2026-2028, but has said that mining alone will not create all the jobs the economy needs.

The International Monetary Fund approved a 38-month, $417 million loan programme for Guinea on Tuesday. It has urged the country to manage volatile mining revenue through clear fiscal rules and greater transparency.
FUND TO GET 30% OF SIMANDOU REVENUE
Under the law, the fund will receive 30% of revenue from Simandou. It will also get 5% of tax and other revenue from mining projects that start after the law takes effect.

The government expects Simandou to double its tax revenue, while the fund will be designed to stop that money being wasted and to avoid Dutch disease, the official said, referring to the economic damage caused when a country is over-reliant on one source of income.

The fund has three goals: diversifying the economy, saving for future generations and cushioning the economy against shocks. It will invest the diversification money mostly domestically, in sectors such as agriculture, energy, transport and mineral processing. Outside asset managers will invest the rest mainly abroad.
Doumbouya, a former special forces commander, seized power in a 2021 coup and won a presidential election in December 2025.
The fund's board will draw up its strategy. A committee of ministers and civil society representatives, headed by Doumbouya, will then approve it.
Seven of the nine board members will be independent and may be foreigners. The other two will represent the finance ministry and the central bank.
